messages.subject: [statnet_help] solution for egocentric density at any distance
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] solution for egocentric density at any distance
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

After my mailing yesterday, I plowed through and wrote a function to  
do what I was looking for. I didn't quite understand the  
neighborhood() function at first, but once I thought more about it, I  
realized that I could do what I was looking for. Here's my code  
(apologies if it's ugly):

#Returns nbddensity, a matrix of egocentric densities for each node in  
a "net" for each distance from 1 to "distance"
nbd_density <- function(net, distance) {	
	
	size <- network.size(net)
	nbddensity <- matrix(nrow = size, ncol = distance)
	nbd <- neighborhood(net, distance, neighborhood.type="total",  
mode="graph", return.all=TRUE, partial = FALSE)
	
	for (i in 1:distance) {
		for (j in 1:size) {
			adj_m <- as.matrix(net[c(nbd[i,j,]==1),c(nbd[i,j,]==1)])
			ifelse (length(as.vector(adj_m)) == 1, nbddensity[j,i] <- 0,
				nbddensity[j,i] <- network.density(as.network.matrix(adj_m,  
matrix.type="adjacency")))
			}
		}	
	nbdensity	
	}

-Michael

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] commented and edited code from last post
messages.body_plain:
Last post on this thread - there was a bug in my function and it  
wasn't very well commented, so here it is. If anyone can think of  
something simpler and faster, that would be great! This is a pretty  
time consuming little function.

-Michael

******

#Function returning nbddensity, a matrix of egocentric neighborhood  
densities for
#each node in a network from distance 1 to "distance"
nbd_density <- function(net, distance) {	
	# Initializing objects
	size <- network.size(net)
	nbddensity <- matrix(nrow = size, ncol = distance)
	
	#Get neighborhoods
	nbd <- neighborhood(net, distance, neighborhood.type="total",  
mode="graph", return.all=TRUE, partial = FALSE)
	
	#Nested loop which creates adjancency matrix for each node in a  
network, then calculates
	#its density and deposits the value in a matrix. Repeated for each  
order up to supplied value distance
	for (i in 1:distance) {
		for (j in 1:size) {
			adj_m <- as.matrix(net[c(nbd[i,j,]==1),c(nbd[i,j,]==1)])
			ifelse (length(as.vector(adj_m)) == 1, nbddensity[j,i] <- 0, #If  
isolate, density = 0, not 1
				nbddensity[j,i] <- network.density(as.network.matrix(adj_m,  
matrix.type="adjacency")))
			}
		}	
	nbddensity	 #return nbddensity matrix,
}

messages.subject: [statnet_help] memory limit
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

Another question: I'm working with a set of networks ranging from  
~400-5000 nodes. I'm running a simple program to calculate basic node- 
level stuff, just three different centrality measures. When I run my  
program on my office's UNIX server, the program inevitably crashes  
with the error "memory exhausted{limit reached?)". I've checked the  
memory limits on the server and they are all "unlimited" except for  
stacksize which is 10240 kbytes. Any suggestions? I'm pasting my code  
below in case maybe it's my code's fault.

-Michael

#APSC_nodes = list of nodes and attributes for each subnetwork in  
APSC_comp
#APSC_comp = list of networks (which are largest components of other  
networks)

APSC_centrality <- list()	

for (i in 1) {
	size <- network.size(APSC_comp[[i]])
	
	#Component nodes indexing
	comp_nodes <- APSC_nodes[[i]][APSC_comp[[i]] %v% "vertex.names",1]
	
	#Precalc geodesic distance matrix
	gd <- geodist(APSC_comp[[i]], predecessors = TRUE)
	
	#PCP node level statistics
	degree <- degree(APSC_comp[[i]], gmode = "graph")
	degree_cent <- degree/(size-1)
	
	#Centrality measures
	between_std <- betweenness(APSC_comp[[i]], nodes = NULL, gmode =  
"graph", cmode = "undirected", geodist.precomp = gd)
	between_std_norm <- 2*between_std/((size-1)*(size-2))
	close <- closeness(APSC_comp[[i]], nodes = NULL, gmode = "graph",  
cmode = "undirected", geodist.precomp = gd)

	
	#Collate into list of dataframes for all nodes and PCPs
	APSC_centrality[[i]] <- cbind(APSC_nodes[[i]][comp_nodes,], degree,  
degree_cent, between_std, between_std_norm, close) 	
}

)

messages.subject: [statnet_help] memory limit
messages.body_plain:
Michael,

I've run into memory problems in the past as well, albeit on a Windows rather 
than unix platform. You've probably already looked at this info, but here are 
some helpful pages:

help(Memory) #note this is case sensitive
help(memory.limit)
help("Memory-limits")

I can't speak for unix platforms, but for Windows platforms memory limits appear 
to be a combination of both OS and R limitations: apparently 32-bit
Windows by default caps user processes at 2G, and R by default requests 1/2G
less than the max; 64-bit Windows caps at 4G by default, and again R by default
requests 1/2G less. The user can increase the available memory using 
memory.limit(size=####) up to the maximum allowed by the OS.

Hopefully someone with unix experience can offer more helpful advice specific to 
your problem.

My work-around has been to split my simulations into smaller batches, extract 
the information I need, and concatenate the results into a new workspace.

Cheers,
David

I hope this email finds you well.  

 

I'd like to estimate the popularity returns to membership in a peer group,
that are "net" of an individual's characteristics.  That is, I want to
distinguish "a group of popular people" from a "popular group."

 

My initial instinct was to specify something like a P1 model, with
individual attractiveness parameters, reciprocity, etc. plus "target group"
parameters (nodeifactor).  But, of course, there is a linear dependency here
that makes such a model unidentified.

 

So, any suggestions for how to capture the popularity due to group
membership?

 

Thanks bunches, 

Jim Moody

Duke Sociology

messages.body_plain:
James,

   This is just a shot in the dark, but could you try specifying a model 
that identifies differences in transitive closure for triads that either 
do or do not include ingroup members?

   If i & j are both members of the target group, then if the "group" is 
important in terms of attractiveness judgements on the part of third 
parties, than I guess I'd expect to see a lot of closed triads:

   j -> i, k -> j, k -> i

and not so many open triads:

   j -> i, k -> j

   What I'm thinking is that if j is a member of a popular subgroup, her 
liking i makes i all the more attractive to k.  I guess this would only 
make sense if what you mean by "a popular subgroup" is "a group whose 
membership plays an important role in defining what's popular".

   It just seems tricky to me to get at this without having some relatively 
process-oriented account for popularity.  I'm not sure if this is the 
mechanism that you had in mind...

- chris
